svg.title: Eight ways to play four parts
svg.desc: Eight timelines contrast simultaneous parts, regular turns, complete cycles, random turns, and longer random packets.

g.text: Read left to right. Colored = playing. Blank = waiting.
Same four parts in every example; extra bass and echoes in Space.
Give the four parts softer sounds, then add bass and echoes.
All parts play together. Echoes make the sound feel wider.
Also playing: a low bass. Echoes repeat the sound softly on the left and right.
Four square-wave sounds at once. A plain, loud starting point.
Four filled rows = four notes sounding together.
One generator: tune, chord note, tune, next chord note...
The tune gets 50% of the time. The repeating pattern can buzz.
3. LESS CHORD: more time for the tune
Keep taking turns, but shorten the chord notes' turns.
The tune gets 75% of the time; the whole chord shares 25%.
Same idea, but wait for the whole high/low wave before switching.
A turn can move a little to avoid cutting a wave in half.
Change note at the next rising edge.
Pick the next part by chance. No repeating turn order.
Lots of tiny, uneven turns can sound like crackling.
Draw a part, let it play 4-12 complete waves, then draw again.
Longer turns give the ear more time to recognize each note.
Give each part its own square-wave generator. Add their sounds.
Everyone plays together again, with a quieter chord behind the tune.
Paler chord strips mean lower volume, not less playing time.
Illustrated rules, not measured waveforms. Row colors identify parts, not loudness (except where noted).
